title: Duas for parents seeking a spouse for their child
excerpt: For the mother and father praying quietly through a long search: the duas Shia parents have traditionally turned to, the moments and places they turn to them, and the conduct that makes a parent's prayer a support to their child rather than a weight.

body.x: There is a particular kind of prayer that parents know well: the one said quietly, over years, for a son or daughter who is ready to marry and has not yet found the person. It is said at the end of namaz, in the car outside the imambara, at the zarih in Karbala if life takes you there. It is rarely dramatic. It is a mother asking, again, for her child's life to open. This guide gathers the duas Shia parents have traditionally turned to, the places and moments they have turned to them, and — just as important — the conduct that makes a parent's dua a support to their child rather than a weight on them.
The dua at the centre of it
The verse most parents reach for first is from Surah al-Furqan (25:74), where the servants of the Most Merciful pray for their families:
"Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and our offspring the comfort of our eyes, and make us leaders for the God-conscious."

Notice what the verse actually asks for. Not a wedding, not a date, not relief from relatives' questions — comfort of the eyes: a spouse and children who become a source of settled joy. Parents who recite it for an unmarried child are asking for exactly the right thing, and asking for it in the right order. Many parents make it part of their daily wird after prayer, sometimes for years, and it does not wear out with use. Alongside it, parents ask in their own words — in Urdu, Farsi, Arabic, English, whatever language their heart thinks in — for a spouse of deen and akhlaq, for doors to open, for the search to end in a home built on mawadda and rahma, affection and mercy. A dua does not need to be famous to be heard. The parent's own words, specific and honest — naming their child's loneliness, their child's goodness — are among the most sincere supplications there are.
Where parents pray: majlis, ziyarat and the blessed times

Shia life gives parents a calendar of moments when hearts are soft and gatherings are full. Parents pray for their children's rishtas during majalis, and it is common — and entirely in the spirit of the gathering — to ask the congregation to join in a dua for all the young people of the community who are searching; a parent who cannot bring themselves to name their own child aloud can intend them within that collective prayer. The nights of Qadr in Ramadan, Friday and the time of Friday prayer, and the moments after obligatory namaz are all times parents traditionally hold onto. Many recite Dua al-Tawassul, turning to the Prophet and his household (as) as intercessors, and Ziyarat Ashura finds its way into many homes during a hard search. Those who travel for ziyarat — to Karbala, Najaf, Mashhad or Qom — almost always carry this one intention with them, and parents who cannot travel ask travelling friends to remember their child at the shrine. None of this is a formula. It is simply parents using every door their tradition opens.
Sadaqah: the prayer your hands say

Alongside words, parents give. Sadaqah made quietly with this intention — money to a family in difficulty, food served at a majlis, a contribution to a young couple's wedding costs — is understood across the tradition as a prayer acted out. Some parents make a nazr, a vow to give or to feed people when the rishta is settled; a vow is a serious thing and should be made thoughtfully and fulfilled exactly, so families often take advice before making one. There is one form of sadaqah parents sometimes overlook because it costs no money: helping another family's search. The mother who passes a good biodata to the right home, the father who makes an introduction at the imambara — they are spending their own network on someone else's child, and parents who do this during their own child's search often find the community remembers. Generosity in this season is never wasted, whatever it returns.
The conduct that belongs with the dua

A dua said at tahajjud can be undone at breakfast. Parents who are praying for a rishta carry the search best when their conduct matches their prayer: no sighing commentary at every family gathering, no comparisons with the cousin who married at twenty-two, no despair performed in front of the child, who is usually carrying more of this than they show. Guard their privacy as you would guard their honour — a biodata forwarded without their knowledge, a photograph passed around a WhatsApp group, teaches them to hide the search from you. Keep the questions gentle and the door open: 'Is there anything you would like us to do?' lands very differently from 'Has anything happened yet?' And hold your own hope as a discipline. Children read their parents' faces for a verdict on their worth; a parent who prays calmly and lives normally gives them the steadiness to search well.
Praying for them — never instead of them

The final thing, and the one that gives all the others their meaning: your dua opens doors, but your child walks through them — or does not. A parent's prayer is for a spouse their child will choose with a whole heart, not for the child's resistance to wear down. The wali's role in our tradition is protection and blessing, not possession; a rishta accepted under pressure, however fervently it was prayed for, begins with a crack in it. So pray for the right person and for your child's eyes to recognise them. Pray for your own patience. And when someone does appear, let your dua change its tense — from asking, to gratitude, to praying for the young couple as they begin. Parents who pray this way usually find their children bring them into the search earlier, trust them with the truth sooner, and lean on the prayer instead of bracing against it. That is what the dua was always for.
